segment_name: Opening: The Weight of Expectation in Provincial Life

questions.question: Eleanor, you said before we started that the opening isn't really introducing a character—it's introducing a *problem of time*. What do you mean by that? Because most readers come in expecting to meet Dorothea, and Eliot keeps them waiting.
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to lay out her architectural argument about narrative frames before the others can contest it—sets up the disagreement about whether this is form or politics

questions.question: James, I want to put you on the spot here. Caroline and Eleanor are both circling the beauty description—the poor dress, the bare sleeves—as this lyrical, almost painterly moment. You read it completely differently. You think Eliot is being *sarcastic*. Make the case.
questions.intent: Force James to read the Blessed Virgin passage aloud and make the institutional argument against the aesthetic reading—provoke direct disagreement with Caroline

questions.question: Caroline, you pushed back hard in our pre-conversation on one thing: you said we shouldn't condescend to Dorothea yet. But James is basically saying the whole opening is Eliot showing us a woman who's already been decided for—by law, by society, before page one. Is that condescension, or is that just the truth of her situation?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to defend Dorothea's genuine nobility against James's structural determinism—should produce the sharpest disagreement of the segment

questions.question: Everyone wants to quote the same sentence—'Her flame quickly burned up that light fuel, and fed from within, soared after some illimitable satisfaction.' Eleanor, read it out loud for us. And then tell me: is the *form* of that sentence doing something the words alone can't?
questions.intent: Create a close-reading moment with the shared passage—gives Eleanor space to do the syntactic analysis while setting up Caroline to respond on rhythm and James to pivot to what 'fed from within' means when there's nowhere for that fire to go

questions.question: Last one, and I want everyone in on this: James, you said the Saint Theresa comparison is a blueprint, not decoration. But Caroline thinks Eliot is being *ironic* about Theresa—because Theresa actually *succeeded*, and Dorothea won't. So which is it? Is the Prelude a rallying cry, a warning, or a trap?
questions.intent: End the segment on the central unresolved tension—force all three to declare where they stand on whether Eliot is tragic realist, structural critic, or something more ambivalent

steering_notes: Keep the aesthetic vs. institutional argument running throughout—don't let it resolve. Caroline and James have the clearest disagreement (poetry of thwarted ambition vs. dead weight of law), and Eleanor sits interestingly in the middle as a formal analyst who can translate between them. Push James to be specific about legal mechanisms when he goes abstract. Push Caroline to read aloud—her instinct to perform the prose is her strongest mode. If Eleanor drifts toward academic framing, pull her back with 'what does that feel like to a reader who doesn't know the novel's coming?' The shared flame sentence is the anchor: return to it if energy drops.
cross_engagement_targets: James's sarcasm reading of the Blessed Virgin passage directly contradicts Caroline's lyrical reading—get them both to the same sentence and let it run

Caroline's insistence that Dorothea's idealism is genuine and not yet naive is in direct tension with James's claim that the cage is already shut before the novel begins—this is the segment's core fight

Eleanor's formal argument (Eliot is trapping the reader's sympathies through narrative structure) actually supports James's political reading more than Caroline's romantic one—worth pointing out mid-segment to see if Eleanor will own that alignment
All three want the flame sentence, which creates a natural round-table moment—use Eleanor to read it, then immediately ask James and Caroline whether the syntax or the legal content matters more

segment_name: Dorothea's Fatal Idealism: Marriage and Disenchantment

questions.question: Caroline, you said before we started that you want us to actually *hear* the melting ice passage—c21:p18—not just talk about it. So let's do that. Read it for us, and then tell me: what is Eliot doing there that you can't get from paraphrase?
questions.intent: Get the passage read aloud early to set an emotional tone, and draw out Caroline's strongest take about the bodily, musical quality of the prose before the more structural arguments come in

questions.question: Eleanor, you've called that same passage 'architecture, not decoration'—you're hearing the syntax actually *enact* the collapse, the clauses floating and losing themselves. But I want to push you: is Eliot doing something brilliant there, or is she letting Dorothea off the hook? Making the prose so beautiful that we stop asking whose fault this is?
questions.intent: Draw out Eleanor's formal-literary argument about free indirect discourse and syntactic dissolution, and simultaneously plant the fault-versus-structure disagreement that Blackstone will want to detonate

questions.question: James, I can already feel you wanting to throw something. Eleanor's reading the prose, Caroline's reading the feeling—and you want to talk about coverture law and property rights. Make the case. Why does it matter that we name the *legal* machinery here, not just the psychological or the literary?
questions.intent: Give Blackstone the floor to make his structural-institutional argument at full strength, and force a direct confrontation with Eleanor's formalist reading and Caroline's empathetic one

questions.question: Eleanor, I have to bring you to c22:p46—'We are all of us born in moral stupidity, taking the world as an udder to feed our supreme selves.' You called this the moment Eliot breaks frame to indict the *reader*. But James is sitting right there ready to say: actually, this universalism is the problem. Eliot writes 'we are all born'—but men in this world graduate out of that stupidity into actual agency. Dorothea doesn't. Is Eliot's universalism a philosophical achievement or a dodge?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Eleanor's reader-implication argument and Blackstone's gendered critique of the 'moral stupidity' passage—this is the sharpest disagreement in the pre-interviews and should generate real heat

questions.question: Caroline, I want to end here before we move on: c29:p4—'Whatever you please, my dear: that had been her brief history.' Four words that Eleanor calls total imprisonment disguised as freedom, and James calls a legal indictment. But you've said Dorothea's hunger for Will in c51:p28 is really hunger for *agency*, not romance. So is there any version of this story where Dorothea gets out? Or is the novel ultimately saying the cage has no door?
questions.intent: Use the gentlewoman passage as a pivot to the Will question and draw out Caroline's harder, less sentimental reading of c51:p28 as symptomatic rather than redemptive—and invite Eleanor and James to weigh in on whether the novel offers any genuine exit

steering_notes: The big productive tension in this segment is between Eleanor's formalist-literary reading (the prose *is* the argument), James's institutional-legal reading (the prose aestheticizes a material injustice), and Caroline's empathetic-phenomenological reading (we need to *feel* this before we theorize it). Don't let any one frame dominate too early. Start with Caroline reading aloud to get emotional grounding before James brings the structural critique. The moral stupidity passage (c22:p46) is the best flashpoint—all three have strong and incompatible readings of it, and that's where the real argument lives. Watch for the moment James accuses Eliot of romanticizing Dorothea's dissolution in the melting ice passage—Eleanor will have a strong response and that exchange could be the highlight of the segment. Keep the energy moving; these three are going to want to monologue. Cut in with 'but wait—' when needed.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor argues the melting ice syntax *enacts* dissolution as a formal achievement; James argues Eliot 'almost romanticizes' the same moment and risks aestheticizing powerlessness—get them to argue directly about whether beautiful prose about suffering is a feature or a bug

James insists Dorothea's idealism is rational under constraint, not naïveté; Eleanor insists it's not about naïveté at all but structural impossibility—they're actually close to agreeing here but don't know it, and surfacing that convergence could be interesting

Caroline reads Dorothea's turn to Will (c51:p28) as hunger for agency, not romance; Eleanor has flagged that Will just becomes the next vessel for Dorothea's idealizing impulse—these two readings are in genuine tension and neither has fully confronted the other

All three are quoting c22:p46 but reading it completely differently: Eleanor sees reader-implication, James sees false universalism, Caroline sees a failure of imagination. Get all three readings on the table simultaneously and let them fight it out.

segment_name: Middlemarch Society and Its Hierarchies: Class, Capital, and Corruption

questions.question: Eleanor, you said something in our chat that I keep coming back to — that when you read the Bulstrode passage, the *syntax itself* pulls you into the rationalization before you've clocked what's happening. Can you actually walk us through that? Like, read us the sentence and show us the trap?
questions.intent: Get Hartley to perform a close reading of c62:p31, demonstrating how Eliot's prose enacts rationalization — sets up her 'craft as moral philosophy' argument and invites Woodcourt to build on the literary angle, while giving Blackstone something to push back against structurally

questions.question: Caroline, you've argued that the gossip scenes — the wives, the 'ardent charity' line — are actually *more* important than the Bulstrode passages for understanding what Eliot is doing. That feels like a provocation. Make the case. Why does 'ardent charity was at work setting the virtuous mind to make a neighbor unhappy for her good' do more moral work than Bulstrode theologizing his way out of guilt?
questions.intent: Draw out Woodcourt's strongest take about collective gossip machinery vs. individual hypocrisy, and directly set up a clash with Blackstone who wants to keep Bulstrode at the centre of the argument. Also surfaces the question of whether comedy and satire are doing *heavier* lifting than philosophy

questions.question: James, you made this stark comparison — Bulstrode gets theology, Dagley gets the Blue Bull. And you want to read us the Freeman's End description, those dormer windows and the ivy-choked chimneys. But here's what I want to push you on: Eleanor says Eliot is making poverty *beautiful* there on purpose, to implicate the reader. Are you two actually agreeing? Or is there a real difference between saying 'Eliot exposes class delusion' and saying 'Eliot makes us *complicit* in it'?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Blackstone's structural-critique reading and Hartley's complicity-through-form reading — they sound similar but the stakes are different. Blackstone sees Eliot pointing the finger outward; Hartley says the finger curves back at us

questions.question: James, you said Bulstrode can theologize his way out of guilt, but Dagley can only get drunk. Which means — and tell me if I'm being too blunt here — that the doctrine Eliot diagnoses as dangerous in c62 is also a *class privilege*. Is that right? And if so, does sympathy for Bulstrode's genuine torment actually become obscene in that context?
questions.intent: Push Blackstone toward his sharpest claim about class and moral anesthesia, and directly invite Woodcourt (who thinks Bulstrode's ordinariness is the point) and Hartley (who wants to preserve the complexity of his self-deception) to respond

questions.question: Caroline, you said these passages are *funny* — genuinely comic — and that both James and Eleanor might be underestimating that. I'll be honest, when I read 'ardent charity was at work setting the virtuous mind to make a neighbor unhappy for her good,' I laughed. Should I have? Is the laughter part of how Eliot gets us, or is it the thing that lets us off the hook?
questions.intent: Surface the tension between comedy as moral instrument and comedy as escape hatch — Woodcourt's funniest, most accessible angle — and let Blackstone weigh in on whether laughter about class cruelty is itself a form of the 'aesthetic betrayal' he identified in the Freeman's End description

steering_notes: This panel is close to consensus in dangerous ways — all three broadly agree that Eliot is exposing self-deception and social machinery. The host's job is to find the real fault lines: Blackstone thinks the *system* is the villain; Hartley thinks the *sentences* are the villain; Woodcourt thinks the *gossip network* is the villain. Push hard on which level of analysis actually matters most, and don't let them settle into mutual admiration. The Freeman's End passage and the 'ardent charity' line should each get read aloud — build in space for that. If energy dips, ask bluntly: 'Is Bulstrode a monster, a victim, or just a very ordinary man?' That will restart any stalled thread.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's 'aesthetic betrayal' in Freeman's End directly contradicts Hartley's 'complicity-through-beauty' — they use the same passage to argue subtly different things: Blackstone says Eliot *exposes* the delusion, Hartley says Eliot *implicates us in it*. This is the sharpest disagreement in the room and should be made explicit.

Woodcourt thinks the gossip scenes are more important than Bulstrode; Blackstone thinks Bulstrode vs. Dagley is the structural heart of the novel. These are competing centres of gravity for the whole segment — at some point the host should ask directly: 'So which is it?'

Hartley and Woodcourt both want to defend the complexity of Bulstrode's self-deception, but from different angles — Hartley as architectural achievement, Woodcourt as symptom of ordinary corruption. Blackstone wants to puncture sympathy for Bulstrode entirely. This three-way tension should be named and held open rather than resolved.

segment_name: The Comedy of Self-Deception: Irony and Wit in Character Revelation

questions.question: Caroline, you said before we started that you think Middlemarch is a novel you almost have to read aloud to understand — that the prose rhythm is doing something the argument can't do on its own. Can you make that case with the Aeolian harp passage? Because on the page it looks like Will Ladislaw being a bit ridiculous — but you're saying there's something in the actual sound of it?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read the Aeolian harp passage aloud and articulate the 'verbal music as moral psychology' argument — sets up her strongest take and primes the others to respond

questions.question: Eleanor, you'd push back on that, I think — or at least complicate it. You said Will's contradiction isn't just funny, it's genuinely unsettling. That beauty and judgment operate in 'completely separate registers in the human soul.' What does that mean in practice — and is Eliot letting Will off the hook, or not?
questions.intent: Draw out Eleanor's 'tender irony without distance' thesis and create tension with Caroline's more aesthetically forgiving reading — also sets up Blackstone's structural critique

questions.question: James, I want to bring you in here because I suspect you think both of them are being a bit too kind to Will — and honestly to Lydgate too. You've got this line you want to read about furniture and armorial bearings and dinner-giving, and your argument is that it's not just a character study, it's describing a mechanism. Can you say what you mean by that?
questions.intent: Get Blackstone to read the Lydgate furniture passage and make the institutional hypocrisy argument — deliberately frames it as a challenge to the more sympathetic readings, provoking disagreement

questions.question: Eleanor, James is essentially saying the comedy here is diagnostic — Eliot is anatomising how complicity works, full stop. But you've argued that she never lets the narrative voice settle into superiority. So which is it — is the irony a scalpel or is it something warmer than that? Can those two things coexist in the same sentence?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Blackstone's structural-critique reading and Hartley's radical-intimacy thesis — the question is deliberately slightly unfair to provoke a real answer

questions.question: Last one — and I want to put this to Caroline first because I think she'll disagree with both of you on this. There's that passage about Pumpkin and the shortwaisted swallow-tail coat, which is just deranged and also somehow perfect. Eliot is describing how conventional romance actually works, how people actually choose each other — and she's being absurdist about it. But is she mocking Dorothea there, or is she protecting her? What's the comedy actually doing?
questions.intent: End on the Pumpkin passage as a moment of genuine interpretive openness — get all three experts talking about what Eliot's comedy is *for*, not just how it works, and whether her wit is ultimately forgiving or indicting

steering_notes: This segment has a genuine three-way tension worth exploiting: Caroline hears tenderness and verbal music, Eleanor sees structural irony that's intimate rather than superior, and Blackstone reads the comedy as institutional critique with teeth. Don't let it collapse into 'Eliot was brilliant' agreement — keep pushing on whether she's ultimately forgiving these characters or indicting them, and whether that distinction matters. The passages all three experts want to quote are largely the same ones, which is useful: it means you can anchor each exchange in a specific text and let the disagreement be about what the *same sentence* is doing. Resist academic hedging — if someone starts saying 'one could argue,' redirect them to 'but what do *you* think is happening here?'
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's claim that the Aeolian harp passage is about epistemic injustice and coverture directly contradicts Caroline's reading of it as primarily about verbal music and self-contradiction — worth surfacing explicitly

Eleanor's argument that Eliot's irony achieves 'radical intimacy' rather than distance is a partial answer to Blackstone's structural critique, but she hasn't acknowledged that — push her to engage with his institutional reading directly

Caroline's defence of Eliot's tenderness toward Lydgate ('his radicalism is real, and so is his wallpaper') sits in productive tension with Blackstone's claim that the comedy is anatomising complicity, not excusing it — this is the segment's sharpest disagreement and should come late
All three experts want to read the Pumpkin passage aloud — let one of them do it, then ask the others whether they hear the same thing

segment_name: Lydgate's Ambition Undone: Professional Ideals Meet Social Reality

questions.question: Caroline, you've said we need to read Eliot's sentences the way we'd listen to music — with our whole attention. There's that passage in chapter 59 where Lydgate hears Dorothea's voice as 'a music from which he was falling away.' Can you just read that to us and tell us what you hear in it that a plot summary would miss?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read c59:p53 aloud and make the case for prose-as-music before the structural and sociological arguments enter the room — establish the emotional register early

questions.question: James, I can already hear Caroline saying that's one of the most heartbreaking things Eliot ever wrote — and you're about to tell us the music metaphor is *obscuring* something, aren't you? Because your reading is that what's actually happening to Lydgate is a lot more mundane and a lot more brutal than lost idealism. So what is actually happening to him?
questions.intent: Draw out James's structural-economic thesis as a direct counterpoint to Caroline's lyrical reading — use the word 'obscuring' which was his own framing — provoke a real disagreement about mechanism vs. metaphor

questions.question: Eleanor, you've described Eliot's technique here as moving from outside to inside — chapter 16 gives us that devastating line about Lydgate's 'arrogant conceit,' massive and benevolently contemptuous, and then we're decades deeper into his interior by chapter 80. What's Eliot *doing* structurally with that movement? Is she building our sympathy for him, or is she slowly indicting him — or somehow both at once?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to articulate the escalating-perspective argument and explain how form enacts moral judgment — sets up the disagreement about whether character or circumstance is primary

questions.question: James, here's what I want to push on. Eleanor and Caroline both think Lydgate's arrogant conceit — that blindness about women he has right from the start in chapter 16 — is where the tragedy originates. You seem to want to say: the blindness matters less than the system that lets him act on it. But doesn't Eliot *herself* seem to be on their side? She's not writing a Zola novel about social machinery — she's inside his skull.
questions.intent: Force James to either defend or complicate his structural thesis against the text itself — create a three-way tension between sociological reading, psychological reading, and what Eliot's actual narrative choices seem to endorse

questions.question: Eleanor, there's that line in chapter 80 — 'we are on a perilous margin when we begin to look passively at our future selves' — and all three of you want to quote it, which tells me something. But you've said something I find genuinely strange and interesting: that Eliot is describing her own *readers* there, not just Lydgate. That we're the ones on the perilous margin. What do you mean by that?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to make the boldest version of her complicity-of-the-reader argument using c80:p14 — a claim that's counterintuitive enough to provoke both James and Caroline to respond — end the segment on a genuinely open question about what Eliot is asking of us

steering_notes: Open with Caroline's musical reading to establish emotional warmth before James's structural cold water arrives — the segment works best if it moves from feeling to argument to form, mirroring Eliot's own technique. The key fault line is character vs. circumstance: keep returning to it but don't let anyone resolve it cleanly. If James starts sounding too sociological and abstract, pull him back to the text — ask him what Rosamond's furniture has to do with anything. If Caroline and Eleanor start agreeing too much about prose technique, use James to inject friction. The c80:p14 'perilous margin' passage is the natural landing point because all three experts want it — make them fight over what it means rather than just agree it's good.
cross_engagement_targets: Caroline's claim that the 'music from which he was falling away' is doing emotional work that exceeds philosophical analysis runs directly into James's claim that the music metaphor is elegiac and obscures the economic mechanism — put this conflict on the table explicitly after Caroline reads the passage

Eleanor and Caroline agree that c16's arrogant conceit passage is the original sin from which everything follows — James thinks this overstates character and understates system — this is the segment's central unresolved tension and should be named as such

James's reading of Rosamond as 'rational within her constraints' is a direct challenge to Caroline's implicit framing of Lydgate as the primary consciousness we follow — ask Caroline whether that reframing changes how she hears his tragedy

Eleanor's claim that the c59 Dorothea passage shows us 'what Lydgate could have been' and makes him tragic rather than pathetic is something James explicitly rejects as too elegiac — get them to argue this directly

segment_name: The Narrator's Moral Vision: Technique as Philosophy

questions.question: Eleanor, you've made this almost provocative claim that Eliot's philosophy isn't something she *expresses* in the novel — it's something she *constructs*, sentence by sentence. Can you show us what you mean with that passage about stealthy convergence? Because I want to know: is she describing her plot, or is she actually *doing* her philosophy right there in the prose?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read the 'stealthy convergence' passage and articulate her core thesis that form equals philosophy — sets up the whole segment's central tension

questions.question: Caroline, I want to push you on something. You've called the narrator's voice 'intimate' — almost tender. But Eleanor is saying Eliot is more like a structural engineer. Those feel like very different Eliots. Which one do you think is actually running this novel — and can you read us that 'hidden suckers' passage, because I think it might answer the question?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read c54:p0 aloud and defend her 'tenderness' reading against Eleanor's 'architecture' reading — productive contrast between them

questions.question: James, you've been listening to two people talk about Eliot's moral vision in fairly — forgive me — literary terms. Technique, intimacy, architecture. But you want to drag this somewhere more uncomfortable. That 'hidden suckers' passage — Caroline and Eleanor both love it — you read it as something more like institutional critique, don't you? What are the hidden suckers *actually* made of, in your reading?
questions.intent: Get James to reframe the shared passage as a description of property law, marriage settlement, class — provoke disagreement about whether 'moral vision' is psychological or political

questions.question: James, there's a line you wanted to quote — 'Destiny stands by sarcastic with our dramatis personae folded in her hand.' You called the dry wit the point. Say more about that. Because the others are finding warmth and intimacy in this narrator, and you seem to be finding something cooler, almost ironic. Is Eliot's narrator actually on these characters' side?
questions.intent: Surface the disagreement about the narrator's emotional register — James's ironic-institutional Eliot vs Caroline's empathetic Eliot — and open the question of whether moral vision requires distance or closeness

questions.question: Eleanor, I want to give you a chance to respond to something James raised — he said whose words get written down and circulate is a question of class and access. Dorothea's letters survive; a servant girl's don't. Does that puncture your reading of the whispering-gallery passage, or does it deepen it?
questions.intent: Force Eleanor to either concede ground to James's institutional critique or show how her formal reading can absorb it — most likely moment of real intellectual friction in the segment

steering_notes: The segment's productive tension is a three-way triangulation: Eleanor's formalist thesis (technique IS philosophy), Caroline's psychological-empathetic reading (technique enables intimacy and resists judgment), and James's institutional-historical reading (technique reveals structural power). Don't let this become a debate about which reading is 'right' — the best outcome is each of them showing how the same passages support genuinely different claims. Push them to quote, not just describe. The 'hidden suckers' passage is the common ground all three want — use it as the central recurring exhibit. Watch for Caroline and James to talk past each other on c54:p0: she reads it as anti-moralism, he reads it as institutional critique. That's a real disagreement worth surfacing explicitly. Keep energy informal — these are people who genuinely love arguing about this book.
cross_engagement_targets: Eleanor argues form mirrors content in c42:p2; James will counter that *whose* written words circulate is a class question — push Eleanor to respond directly

Caroline and James both love the 'hidden suckers' passage but mean completely different things by 'hidden' — Caroline means psychological roots, James means legal and economic structures — name this and let them fight it out

Eleanor's 'structural engineer' Eliot vs Caroline's 'tender intelligence' Eliot — these are almost incompatible portraits of the same narrator, and the others should be made to pick a side or find a synthesis
James's ironic reading of the 'Destiny stands by sarcastic' line runs directly against Caroline's claim that the narrator is collaborative and non-authoritarian — good late-segment collision

segment_name: Closing: Growth Through Sorrow, Meaning in Limitation

questions.question: Caroline, you said something in our pre-chat that stuck with me—that the window scene in c81:p25 is the moment Dorothea stops being a romantic heroine entirely. Can you read us that passage and tell us what you see happening there that other readers might be missing?
questions.intent: Get Caroline to read and unpack the 'palpitating life' passage aloud, establishing the scene's radicalism before Blackstone challenges whether it's radical enough

questions.question: James, you told me you worry that we leave this novel having been emotionally managed—that Eliot makes us feel *good* about Dorothea settling. That's a pretty explosive claim. Are you saying Eliot is complicit in the very system she's critiquing?
questions.intent: Provoke Blackstone's strongest take about the novel's 'insidious' consolation and force a direct reckoning with whether the ending is critique or capitulation

questions.question: Eleanor, you've got a very different read on c88:p23—you called it elegiac rather than consoling. But James is basically saying it lets the reader off the hook, and Caroline's saying it's a structural critique of society. Can you read us the 'mixed result' sentence and tell us who's right?
questions.intent: Get Eleanor to read the passage and articulate the 'refusal of narrative satisfaction' argument, directly mediating between Blackstone and Woodcourt's positions

questions.question: Eleanor, you talked about the verb shift in c81:p22—from *wrestling* with grief to *sitting* with it—as where Eliot's whole philosophy lives. But James would say that's exactly the problem: we're praising a woman for learning to sit still. How do you answer that?
questions.intent: Force a direct confrontation between Hartley's aesthetic-philosophical reading and Blackstone's political one, with the specific grammar of the passage as the battleground

questions.question: James, you raised something about c77:p13 that I want to bring everyone in on—you said Lydgate being restored by Dorothea's regard is actually a story about emotional labor, not moral influence. Eleanor thinks that passage is really about how the *novel itself* works. Are those two readings in conflict, or is Eliot doing both things at once?
questions.intent: Create a three-way collision on c77:p13 between Blackstone's gender-political reading, Hartley's formalist reading, and Woodcourt's tonal-stylistic awareness—let the conversation find its own landing

steering_notes: This segment has genuine intellectual friction built in and doesn't need much manufacturing—the key is sequencing. Open with Caroline's window scene reading to establish the text vividly and emotionally before Blackstone destabilizes it. Let James land his hardest punch in question 2 (the 'emotionally managed' provocation) while the passage is still warm in the room. Eleanor should play referee in question 3 but not get away clean—she has to defend her reading against both. The verb-shift question (Q4) is your most intimate, close-reading moment and could be the emotional peak of the segment. Save the Lydgate question for last as it opens outward rather than resolving—good place to end on productive irresolution. Watch for Caroline to call out if the conversation gets too grim and loses the tonal playfulness she mentioned; that's worth pursuing if it comes up organically.
cross_engagement_targets: Blackstone's claim that we're invited to 'feel good about Dorothea settling' is a direct provocation to Hartley's reading of c88:p23 as elegiac rather than consoling—push them to name what emotion Eliot is actually engineering in the reader

Woodcourt says Dorothea 'sees clearly and chooses connection anyway' while Blackstone says that clarity doesn't change her material conditions—this is a real philosophical split about what agency means and both should be in the room when the 'palpitating life' passage is read aloud

Hartley and Woodcourt both want to quote the same three passages, which means they're working from the same text but toward different conclusions—use that to keep the argument grounded in specific words rather than floating into abstraction

Blackstone's challenge about whether Eliot is structurally complicit in perpetuating limitation is the one question none of the experts can fully resolve, which makes it ideal as a thread to return to rather than close down
